topic: Foreign investment routes into India: FDI (stake above 10% or a factory) vs FPI (below 10%), the FII/QFI history, the 2014 merger into RFPI with three risk categories, and the P-note detour

concepts.name: two routes of foreign investment: FDI and FPI
FDI route 1: stake above 10% in an Indian company
concepts.prereq_recalled: what a stake in a company is (used, not explained)

concepts.name: FDI route 2: setting up a manufacturing facility in India
why companies choose FDI: no customs duty, cheap labour, friendly policies
concepts.prereq_recalled: customs duty on imported goods (used, not explained)

concepts.name: FII vs QFI: who they were, when allowed, how strictly regulated
concepts.prereq_recalled: SEBI as the market regulator (named, not explained)

concepts.name: 2014 merger of FII and QFI into FPI; everyone re-registers with SEBI
RFPI: the new name for registered FPIs
rule and exception: registered FPIs invest directly; unregistered investors go through them and get P-notes

book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook would define FDI and FPI side by side, then list investor classes and regulations. The video keeps one picture (foreign investors -> India) and grows it as a tree: it splits into FDI and FPI, finishes the FDI branch completely (two routes, one real case each, then why a company would bother), recaps that branch, and only then opens FPI, which it tells as a chain of years (1994 FII, 2011 QFI, 2014 merger, RFPI rename, risk categories). The rule (must register with SEBI) is stated last and immediately followed by its exception (P-notes), which becomes the cliff-hanger for the next video.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Every new piece is one branch hung on the same investor-to-India picture: first by route (stake or factory, above or below 10%), then by investor type, then by year of rule change, and the exception to the last rule closes the video.

narration.density: About 22 new terms or acronyms (FDI, FPI, stake, manufacturing facility, customs duty, production cost, FII, QFI, SEBI, KYC, high net worth individual, merger, the committee, RFPI, category I/II/III, sovereign wealth fund, hedge fund, private equity, securities market, P-note, offshore derivative instrument) in about 7 minutes, about 3 per minute. Heavy for a first look; it works only because every acronym is unpacked at first mention and the tree stays on screen. The second half (FII/QFI/RFPI) feels like a list of regulatory facts rather than an explanation.

talmel_summary: The anchor picture (investor box -> India box) is kept almost all video, and new branches appear with or 1-4 s before their words, so the learner always sees where a new acronym hangs. The fits that teach are few: the factory popping onto the India box, the two panels collapsing into one band at 'merge', the register arrow to the SEBI badge, and the registered vs unregistered investors side by side. Most other changes write the narration as text (definitions, member lists, regulation verdicts, the benefits list), so the screen reads like notes being typed rather than a process being shown.

voice.notes: About 166 words per minute, calm and even, with short pauses between points. Acronyms are read letter by letter and immediately expanded with 'yaani'. Signposts are spoken plainly ('chaliye sabse pehle dekhte hain', 'iske baad agar hum baat karein'). Explanations start with 'dekhiye baat ye hai ki' or 'actually hota kya hai ki'. Percentages and years are read in full ('10% se zyada', 'year 1994'). The word 'twist' near the end is stressed to mark the exception. Ends with a channel plug in the same tone.

game_ideas.player_does: Works an 'investment gate' desk: deal cards arrive (a foreign firm buys 12% of an Indian company, a pension fund buys 3% of shares on the exchange, a foreign phone maker builds a plant, a hedge fund buys 2%) and the learner sends each through the FDI gate or the FPI gate.
game_ideas.process_happens: The chosen route draws on the anchor picture: the elbow 'stake' arrow onto a company, the straight arrow to a new factory, or the arrow through the stock exchange; a stake bar on each card fills to its percent against a marked 10% line.
game_ideas.win: All deals routed correctly; the tree under 'invest' fills both branches.
game_ideas.lose: Sending a 3% buy to FDI shows its stake bar stopping below the 10% line and the deal bouncing back to the FPI gate.
game_ideas.concept: FDI vs FPI (10% line; stake or factory)

game_ideas.player_does: Runs a foreign phone company selling in India and chooses each year: keep shipping phones in, or build a factory in India.
game_ideas.process_happens: Shipped phones pass a customs gate that adds duty to each phone's price; factory phones skip the gate and use cheaper local labour, so their cost tag is lower; a policy card can add a government incentive.
game_ideas.win: Reach the lowest cost per phone, which happens only after choosing the factory (FDI route 2).
game_ideas.lose: Staying with shipping shows the duty stacked on every phone and a rival with a local factory undercutting the price.
game_ideas.concept: why companies choose FDI (customs duty, cheap labour, favourable policies)

game_ideas.player_does: Plays a foreign investor who wants Indian shares: chooses to register with SEBI as an FPI (picking the right risk category for its type) or to skip registration.
game_ideas.process_happens: A registered investor's money flows straight through the exchange to the company and shares come back; an unregistered one is stopped at the SEBI badge and can only hand money to a registered FPI, getting a P-note instead of shares.
game_ideas.win: Place three investor types (a central bank, a pension fund, a hedge fund) in categories I, II, III and get their money to the company by a legal route.
game_ideas.lose: Trying to go direct without registering lights the SEBI badge red and reroutes the money through the FPI with a P-note.
game_ideas.concept: SEBI registration, RFPI categories, P-note route

game_ideas.player_does: Orders cards: FIIs allowed (1994), QFIs allowed (2011), merger into FPI (2014), rename to RFPI, three risk categories.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each card grows the FPI tree: two panels appear, collapse into one band, the chip is relabelled, the three category branches drop down.
game_ideas.lose: Placing the merger before 2011 shows nothing on the QFI side to merge, with a nudge to place QFI first.
game_ideas.concept: history of foreign portfolio investor categories

checks_learned: A threshold in a definition (10% stake) should be drawn as a quantity against a marked line, not only written; the same for a stated stake (77%).
A cause_effect list (benefits of FDI) shown as text bullets should be flagged; each cause needs a picture of the step (goods crossing a customs gate vs made inside).
Every acronym must be unpacked at first mention (E18 does this for all six; enforce it).
A long sub-branch (more than about 90 s) should end with a recap on the anchor picture before the next branch (E18 does this at 130 s; enforce it).
The second side of a contrast (QFI 'fewer regulations') should not appear on screen before the voice has finished the first side.
When the voice names two names for one thing (RFPI officially, FPI in the news), the screen should show both, linked.
A term named in the closing (offshore derivative instrument) must get at least a one-line yaani unpack, even if the detail is deferred.
Real brand logos and real takeover names should be replaced by generic companies in BIE's own lessons.

teaching_best.why: One anchor picture (investors -> invest -> India) is reused for every later idea, so each acronym is a branch of something already seen.
The learner's natural doubt ('what does the company gain?') is voiced and answered with a short cause chain (customs duty, cheap labour, policies).
Recaps both FDI routes on the tree before opening FPI, so the 10% line is fresh when FPI is defined as below it.
The rule (register with SEBI) is followed at once by its exception, shown as two investor kinds side by side with one feeding the other.

teaching_weak.why: The three FDI benefits are a text-only bullet list; no picture of a customs gate, a cost tag or a factory.
FII vs QFI is long text panels (about 74 words on screen); the real difference (strictness of rules) is only red vs green text lines.
The RFPI rename and the three categories are told as facts with no reason why risk category matters to anyone.
The 10% threshold and the 77% stake are never drawn as amounts, so 'above 10%' stays an abstract phrase.
P-notes are named as an 'offshore derivative instrument' without any unpacking before the video ends.
